extracted.intended_audience: novelists and screenwriters seeking a plotting/structure method (writers outlining stories)
extracted.subtask_description: Outlining and plotting fiction using Blake Snyder's Save the Cat 15-beat framework, adapted for novels and screenplays. Provides beat-by-beat descriptions, recommended page/percentage allotments, pacing advice, examples (The Hate U Give), and guidance on using the method as a tool rather than a strict formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image
rubrics_metrics.description: An opening snapshot that instantly introduces us to the present world of the hero (in film a visual image; in a novel a vivid scene that draws the reader in and sets tone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended at ~1% of story (screenplay page 1). Should conjure a vivid scene; often mirrored or contrasted by the Final Image. Example: Starr at a Garden Heights party (The Hate U Give).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated
rubrics_metrics.description: We are introduced to the central theme or lesson of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs early (~5%); should clearly signal the central idea the hero will discover. Example: injustice / 'THUG LIFE' meaning in The Hate U Give (3%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set Up
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduces the hero and their 'ordinary world' and presents crucial details and character flaws to be overcome before the story is shaken up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~1–10% (pages 1–10). Avoid spending too much time on irrelevant backstory; provide enough information for readers to care and to place the story (worldbuilding hints woven into narrative). Inciting incident benchmark: aim for the catalyst within the first ~12,000–13,000 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst
rubrics_metrics.description: Also called the inciting incident: the single major plot point that sets the hero on the course they will pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~10% (screenplay page 12). It must clearly alter the hero's world and create the central problem/quest. Example: Khalil's shooting in The Hate U Give (5%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero hesitates and resists taking action after the catalyst, wrestling with whether to engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~10–25% (page 12–25). Use this beat to show internal conflict and stakes of taking action; it should make the eventual Break Into Two meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Two
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero makes a definitive choice to take on the challenge, moving from Act One into Act Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~25% (screenplay page 25). Marks the protagonist committing to the story’s main conflict (example: Starr presenting as an anonymous witness).

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot introduced early that runs alongside the main plot, typically involving a character who helps the hero’s transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~30% (page 30). Often a romantic interest or a mentor-like figure; it provides emotional lessons and contributes to the hero’s eventual Break Into Three. Example: DeVante in The Hate U Give (32%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games (Promise of the Premise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The portion of the story where the central concept or 'hook' is delivered — what the audience was promised by the premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~30–55% (pages 30–55). May not be literal fun; it’s where the protagonist engages in the main action/conflict (e.g., superhero fights, detective sleuthing). Use to show core attractions of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: A pivotal event that culminates the action of Fun and Games, raising the stakes (often a false victory or major revelation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~50% (page 55). It should change the game for the protagonist — stakes increase and direction shifts. Use to pivot the story’s urgency and escalate conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the Midpoint, tension mounts and things begin to go downhill for the hero; external and internal pressures intensify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~50–75% (pages 55–75). Use this beat to isolate the protagonist, complicate relationships, and narrow options. Example: Starr faces hostility and social fallout (76–85%).

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's rock-bottom moment when everything seems to have failed and hope appears lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~75% (page 75). It should feel like utter defeat (e.g., grand jury decision not to indict). This beat primes the emotional pivot in Dark Night of the Soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul
rubrics_metrics.description: A reflective, despairing beat where the hero reckons with loss and must confront their interior truth before finding a way forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~75–85% (pages 75–85). Use for inward emotional processing that leads to insight for Break Into Three. Example: Starr’s isolation and reflection (86%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Three
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero realizes a crucial truth (often aided by the B Story) and finds renewed motivation and a new strategy to confront the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~80% (page 85). The protagonist transitions from despair to action, armed with lessons learned and clarity of purpose. Example: Starr is galvanized by peaceful protest and decides to speak up (91%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale
rubrics_metrics.description: The climactic sequence in which the hero applies their new awareness to resolve the main conflicts and defeat the antagonistic forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs ~85–110% (pages 85–110). Should tie together plot and emotional arcs; the protagonist's transformation is demonstrated through decisive action. Example: Starr reveals herself publicly and confronts multiple antagonists (92–97%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image
rubrics_metrics.description: A closing snapshot that mirrors or contrasts the Opening Image to show the hero’s transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs at story’s end (~99–100%). Use a visual or scene that makes the change palpable. Example: Starr reflecting on Khalil and her commitment to speak out (100%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat Brevity Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each beat should be describable in one or two sentences to ensure clarity of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snyder: 'If I can’t fill in the blank in one or two sentences — I don’t have a beat yet!' Use short summaries to test whether a beat is fully formed and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended Page/Percentage Allotments (Pacing & Balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended page counts/percentages for each beat (originating from a 110-page screenplay) to monitor pacing and balance across the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided percentages/pages as a diagnostic: they reveal where your story may be sagging or overstuffed. Note: when adapting to novels, these proportions are guidance with wiggle room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use STC as Tool, Not Crutch
rubrics_metrics.description: The beat sheet is a guide to structure — it should aid plotting but not replace the author's instincts or creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid following the outline 'beat for beat' as a shortcut; over-reliance can produce stale work. Balance use of the template with authorial discovery, revision, and rounded character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the Protagonist Sympathetic ('Save the Cat' Moment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a moment early where the protagonist does something that endears them to the audience, so readers root for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be literal or figurative; the key is to create sympathy or emotional investment. Avoid clichés; aim for unique, believable actions that reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story Functionality (Transformation Driver)
rubrics_metrics.description: The B Story's primary function is to provide the hero with emotional lessons and a catalyst for internal change that enables the final victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce the B Story early; use it to teach the protagonist the truth they need at Break Into Three. It should be thematically linked to the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver the Promise of the Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the Fun and Games section actually delivers the core attractions set up by the story concept or hook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what readers expect from your premise and provide scenes that satisfy that expectation while deepening stakes and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midsection/Middle Diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs the middle isn’t working include excessive recap, choppy scene-to-scene transitions, insufficient tension, and lack of character change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixes include increasing conflict/tension, adding or strengthening subplots, clarifying scene goals, and ensuring internal and external motivations advance character change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for Building Tension Toward the Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise stakes emotionally and externally, remove easy escape options, foreshadow developments, and structure unanswered plot-questions to escalate urgency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer obstacles, limit options for the protagonist, up emotional cost, and pace revelations so that stakes compound toward the Finale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Chapter Best Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening must engage quickly, establish a sense of place, and avoid bogging readers down with unnecessary backstory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give readers enough to care (character, voice, inciting action) and place necessary world details sparingly. The opening should ignite some plot, question, or voice within the first chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation Caveat: Screenplay->Novel Proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder’s page-based proportions were designed for a 110-page screenplay; novelists should adapt these percentages with flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reedsy notes 'much more wiggle room' for novels; use percentages as a baseline but adjust for genre, length, and narrative mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial/Cross-Media Consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: STC’s screenwriting origins make its structure familiar and market-friendly to audiences and industry professionals seeking cross-media potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for film/TV adaptation or commercial publication, using STC can make a manuscript feel more translatable and commercially tuned — but weigh artistic goals against marketability.

rubrics_metrics.name: When and How to Break Structure Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can break traditional structure rules, but only after understanding them thoroughly and with deliberate, meaningful intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking the rules is riskier for new authors seeking traditional publication; best attempted after experience and when execution is 'exquisitely' intentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Template Usage for Diagnosing Sagging Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Filling in an STC beat-sheet template lets you instantly see where a story is sagging or misbalanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reedsy provides a fillable template with recommended page allotments/percentages to help identify weak beats and pacing issues; use it to outline quickly and iterate.
